Mandela's Hands

By: Kate Barry | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
The most valuable art work ever produced in South Africa, but it's impossible to sell it

Summary:
In 2003 harmony Gold cast replicas of Nelson Mandela's hands in pure gold. Malcolm Duncan bought the first set of ife-size hands as an investment in a unique artwork that would commemorate Nelson Mandela for all time. Now valued at between $25 and $50 million, he is unable to sell them because of false information on the certificate of authenticity.

Further information:
The limited series of hands was touted as Harmony's latest" beneficiation initiative", and was meant to be donated to the Nelson Mandela Children's Fund. But nothing has gone according to plan: out of the intended 27 sets(one for every year of Mandela's incarceration), only one has been produced. Malcolm Duncan paid R2.5million for the set, but no money was received by the Children's Fund. The contract between Harmony Gold and the Children's Fund Committee, A Touch of Mandela, was never signed. But most importantly the name on the Certificate of Authenticity plaque provided by Harmony s Ross Calder, listing him as a trustee of the Nelson Mandela Trust. Ross Calder has never been a trustee and was widely discredited after he was found to be pocketing proceeds from other Mandela artworks. It is this problem with Ross Calder's name that has made the hands worthless. All interested parties disappear as soon as Malcolm Duncan points out the problem with the Certificate. Harmony Gold has refused to produce another plaque with the correct information, and now Madikizela Mandela, representing House of Mandela, has offered to re-certify the hands for a 15% cut of the proceeds of the sale.

Press Release:


Mandela’s Hands
It’s potentially the most valuable art work ever produced in South Africa. In 2003 Harmony Gold cast pure gold replicas of Madiba’s hands. Today they’re estimated to be worth between 25 and 50 million dollars. The limited series was touted as a Harmony beneficiation initiative, with proceeds to be donated to the Nelson Mandela Children’s Fund. But nothing went according to plan. Why have these treasured hands now become an investment nightmare for the South African who bought the only set produced?


Script:


MANDELA HANDS

V/O: In Alberta, Canada, a big dig is underway. Buried beneath the soil lies a closely guarded secret that is being unearthed at Carte Blanche’s request. This hidden treasure contains what is potentially the most valuable artwork ever to come out of South Africa.

Malcolm: Even after 13 years, every time I pick it up it still feels special to me.

V/O: Malcolm Duncan owns the Mandela Gold Hands, a collection of 3 life-size replicas of the right hand of Nelson Mandela, cast in pure gold. To him Madiba was a hero and he was lucky enough to meet him twice.

Bongani: What was he like?

Malcolm: How are you? I'll never forget it. When he asked how are you he climbed into your soul. He didn't just sit back. He meant what he was saying.

Link: What makes a work of art valuable? I suppose whatever people are willing to pay for it. But the intrinsic value of these Hands comes with the name Nelson Mandela.

V/O: In 2001 Nelson Mandela sketched a series of five humble images that illustrated his life. He then created numerous original artworks, published in limited editions and sold around the world by his art publisher Ross Calder. The series was launched on Robben Island in 2003 and raised millions for charity.

Mandela: "When I initially did the sketches in black chalk, the images looked quite bleak. I then thought that it should be a celebration and introduced the bright and cheery colours.”

V/O: Through his company Touch of Mandela, Calder had the sole rights to market and sell Mandela’s art. In 2003 he came up with the idea of the Hands and approached Harmony Gold. Daan van Heerden was the General Manager at the time.

Daan: We discussed the concept. He came up with the idea that Mandela was in jail for 27-years, let's have 27 of these hands.

V/O: They agreed to manufacture 27 sets of Gold Hands using a technique developed by David Bolam and his colleagues.

Daan: The real secret behind the technique was in the materials they used to allow very high definition.

V/O: They went to Nelson Mandela’s home in Houghton to cast the moulds.

Daan We made two imprints and his hands had to be in the cast for about 20 minutes.

V/O: In attendance was Ross Calder and Nelson Mandela’s longtime lawyer, Ismael Ayob. His role was to ensure that royalties from the artworks would flow back to Madiba.

Link: A cornerstone of Mandela’s legacy is his love for children. And that is what was behind this idea. Harmony Gold was to merely recoup the costs of producing the Golden Hands.

V/O: The profits were to be shared by Ross Calder and the Nelson Mandela Children’s Fund. And Malcolm was excited to be making a donation.

Malcolm: Whatever the gold value was, an equal amount had to be given to charity.

V/O: At the time the gold price was $400 and ounce, and a set of hands weighs almost 10kg

Malcolm: Certainly I wanted it as an investment. I sold whatever I could to raise money to buy whatever was available, because the only set that was available is the set I ordered at the time - the 1990 set, and there was a 1964 fist available so I said give me the fist with that.




V/O: Instead of going through Ross Calder, Malcolm dealt directly with Harmony Gold and paid almost R2.5 million for his 4 pieces. Each hand bears Nelson Mandela’s signature, and the year. The presentation box contains a brass plaque with a history of that year, and another with a certificate of authenticity and authorization. But this is not enough, according to the Curator of Johannesburg’s Everard Read Gallery, Mark Read.

Mark: This is not a certificate this is a brass plaque which was machined on. No-one with their hand applied their signature to it, so there is no recourse in a brass plaque.

Bongani: What about Mandela’s signature on the Hands?

Mark: It’s entirely correct that his signature is there, but it’s a cast-in signature it’s not his signature, he didn’t put it on there. What it’s missing is the edition number which totally explains how many of those there are.

Bongani: What’s wrong with the invoice?

Mark: There should be a piece of paper for each piece, stating exactly what it is and doing the due respect for these pieces. At the moment this is the same as you’d get in a hardware store buying a bunch of nails.

V/O: In 2005 Malcolm Duncan moved to Canada taking the Mandela Hands with him. A few years later he decided to sell them and approached Bonham’s, the London art auctioneers who’ve achieve record prices for South African art – the highest being £3 million Pounds for Irma Stern’s “Arab Priest”.

Malcolm: Bonham’s flew over to Canada, a man by the name of Giles Peppiatt came over and inspected the hands and said fantastic. This I can sell in Russia very easily - £3 to 5 million Pounds.

V/O: Malcolm also appointed an agent in Spain, gallery owner Dr Bridget Orlop.



Bridget: I worked with some other art dealers who approached galleries like the Al-Thani family in Qatar. We approached the Getty Museum - they thought it was a marvelous idea. Then individuals, the private ones wanted the Hands as part of a private collection.

Bongani: What offers were you getting?

Bridget: I had offers up to 35 million Euro.

Bongani: So why didn’t the sale go through?

Bridget: As soon it came to the due diligence, the fact that the name of Ross Calder was on the certificate of identification of each of the boxes, just stalled every deal.

V/O: In 2005 a legal dispute arose between Nelson Mandela, Ismael Ayob, and Ross Calder over Mandela’s lithographs.

Mark: There were questions asked about the signatures looking too similar, and maybe there was a machine involved? Which was vociferously denied by Mr Calder. Was the Children’s Fund, in fact the recipient of the money that people expected them to get?

V/O: Ayob gave a full account of how the money was distributed, but Touch of Mandela was stopped from selling any more artwork involving Mandela’s name. This also impacted on the Golden Hands project.

Daan: There was a legal letter from Mr Ayob that gave us instructions to stop selling the Hands and to return the moulds.

V/O: This means that Malcolm’s Gold Hands are the only ones that were ever made. But the spat left a negative association with the name of Ross Calder. What’s more, on the brass plaque, Ross Calder’s name incorrectly appears as a Trustee of the Nelson Mandela Trust – something he never claimed to be. This was Harmony Gold’s mistake.

Graham: Whether we knew he wasn’t a trustee or not I don't know.

V/O: Graham Briggs is a former CEO of Harmony Gold.

Graham: Whether the people that put that together or not I do not know. I think that the assumption was that he was representing the Children’s Fund.

Mark: So the plaque has incorrect information, and that is very damning for the marketability of these. It’s a body blow to their value.

Malcolm: My dealings were not with Calder. I went straight to Harmony. I paid Harmony. Harmony put them in my hands. So I don’t know why I’m inheriting their problem with the certificate? They should fix the certificate.

Graham: In 2006 it would have been easy to sort that out because we could have re-authenticated completely separately without everyone getting involved in the pubic eye.

V/O: But almost R1 million donation was never received by Ross Calder or the Nelson Mandela Children’s Fund. So what did Harmony Gold do with the money?

Bongani: Can you confirm how much went to the Nelson Mandela Children's Fund?

Graham: Unfortunately not, and because it’s 13 years ago - the company keeps that sort of detailed record for 7 years and after that you can destroy it. We've really hunted for those records.

V/O: Since the death of Nelson Mandela, it seems the value of the Hands has simply sky-rocketed.

Malcolm: Other people who were unaware of the Calder issue offered between $7.5 to $25 million. I flew to Shanghai, went to an auction house, they got three of their experts to examine all the paperwork and photos that I had, and they offered over $50 million.

V/O: But on discovering all the grey areas the offers disappeared.
Link: There’s no question the Mandela Hands are priceless. No other historical figure has been represented and preserved in quite the same way. The conundrum Malcolm Duncan faces is that no one wants to touch them.

Bongani: What would give Malcolm Duncan sufficient provenance in order to sell these Hands at the prices he was offered?

Mark: He needs the certificate stating exactly what they are, how many all signed by a person of unimpeachable integrity who was associated with the process.

Bongani: Let's speculate, what do you think they could fetch finally?

Mark: R35, R40 million would be my guess. I would have to include the Children’s Fund in the huge profit that is being made. Otherwise I really do think that the odour surrounding these Hands will not leave them in the future.

Malcolm: If there is profit to be given I will share it fairly. I hope I’m not a greedy guy.

Graham: Unfortunately not, and because it’s 13 years ago - the company keeps that sort of detailed record for 7 years and after that you can destroy it. We've really hunted for those records. V/O: Since the death of Nelson Mandela, it seems the value of the Hands has simply sky-rocketed. Malcolm: Other people who were unaware of the Calder issue offered between $7.5 to $25 million. I flew to Shanghai, went to an auction house, they got three of their experts to examine all the paperwork and photos that I had, and they offered over $50 million. V/O: But on discovering all the grey areas the offers disappeared. Link: There’s no question the Mandela Hands are priceless. No other historical figure has been represented and preserved in quite the same way. The conundrum Malcolm Duncan faces is that no one wants to touch them. Bongani: What would give Malcolm Duncan sufficient provenance in order to sell these Hands at the prices he was offered? Mark: He needs the certificate stating exactly what they are, how many all signed by a person of unimpeachable integrity who was associated with the process. Bongani: Let's speculate, what do you think they could fetch finally? Mark: R35, R40 million would be my guess. I would have to include the Children’s Fund in the huge profit that is being made. Otherwise I really do think that the odour surrounding these Hands will not leave them in the future. Malcolm: If there is profit to be given I will share it fairly. I hope I’m not a greedy guy.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): The most valuable art work ever produced in South Africa, but it's impossible to sell it
metadata.Summary: In 2003 harmony Gold cast replicas of Nelson Mandela's hands in pure gold. Malcolm Duncan bought the first set of ife-size hands as an investment in a unique artwork that would commemorate Nelson Mandela for all time. Now valued at between $25 and $50 million, he is unable to sell them because of false information on the certificate of authenticity.
metadata.Further information: The limited series of hands was touted as Harmony's latest" beneficiation initiative", and was meant to be donated to the Nelson Mandela Children's Fund. But nothing has gone according to plan: out of the intended 27 sets(one for every year of Mandela's incarceration), only one has been produced. Malcolm Duncan paid R2.5million for the set, but no money was received by the Children's Fund. The contract between Harmony Gold and the Children's Fund Committee, A Touch of Mandela, was never signed. But most importantly the name on the Certificate of Authenticity plaque provided by Harmony s Ross Calder, listing him as a trustee of the Nelson Mandela Trust. Ross Calder has never been a trustee and was widely discredited after he was found to be pocketing proceeds from other Mandela artworks. It is this problem with Ross Calder's name that has made the hands worthless. All interested parties disappear as soon as Malcolm Duncan points out the problem with the Certificate. Harmony Gold has refused to produce another plaque with the correct information, and now Madikizela Mandela, representing House of Mandela, has offered to re-certify the hands for a 15% cut of the proceeds of the sale.
